Federally Qualified Health Centers like HealthLinc exist because Washington’s healthcare system prioritizes bureaucracy over market-driven solutions. While serving 3,000 patients sounds noble, it’s a band-aid on the hemorrhage of federal overreach. These centers rely on HHS grants and 340B drug pricing schemes that let hospitals profit while taxpayers foot the bill.

Real reform would break Big Pharma’s pricing monopolies and slash the red tape that makes community clinics necessary in the first place.

Until then, we’re just subsidizing failure.

Indiana’s R&D tax credit enhancements could be a win—if they’re structured to cut bureaucratic red tape, not subsidize corporate bloat. The state’s existing R&D sales tax exemption already allows 100% write-offs for qualified equipment, but without strict audits, these programs risk becoming slush funds for connected insiders.

Warsaw’s orthopedic manufacturers drive real innovation, but taxpayer dollars must fund breakthroughs—not backroom deals. Let’s see if the “enhancements” prioritize accountability or just more loopholes.

Efficiency isn’t optional—it’s the price of progress.

Rep. Yakym’s bill highlights a critical flaw in Medicare’s bureaucracy: endless delays for life-saving tech. While streamlining approvals is a start, the real issue is systemic. H.R. 3069’s Medicare-for-All framework would amplify this dysfunction by centralizing control, not fixing it.

Cutting red tape is meaningless if D.C. still lets Big Pharma monopolize pricing and regulators drown innovation in compliance costs. True reform requires dismantling the entire graft cycle—where bureaucrats and corporations profit while patients wait.

This bill nibbles at the edges. Until Congress guts the FDA’s 10-year approval marathons and Medicare’s price-fixing schemes, seniors will keep losing.

The real story is buried in the details—see how the system keeps patients waiting: https://t.co/BQB0xv290R

The Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act sounds noble until you read Section 2(c)(1) - mandating CMS spend $10M annually through 2031 just to process paperwork. This "streamlined pathway" creates a $994M deficit spike over 10 years (CBO) while letting bureaucrats pocket $60M in "administrative costs." Breakthrough devices? More like breakthrough billing.

Medicare already hemorrhages $60B annually on medical fraud - this bill adds layers of complexity instead of simplifying access. When FDA rubber-stamps devices, taxpayers shouldn't foot the bill for CMS' redundant reviews.

Cut the middlemen, not just red tape.

Congressional oversight and public scrutiny are overdue—see the full breakdown: https://t.co/4KcBiZioh2
